p: The Romans dated their history from the founding of their city, which they placed in the year seven hundred and fifty-three before Christ, by the twins Romulus and Remus, who had been suckled by a she-wolf, and of whom one murdered the other in a quarrel about a wall. It is a fitting legend for a people whose greatest achievements were the building of walls and the conduct of quarrels. For some two and a half centuries, according to their tradition, Rome was ruled by kings. The last of them, Tarquin the Proud, was driven out, the story says, after his son violated a virtuous noblewoman named Lucretia, and in the year five hundred and nine before Christ the Romans swore never again to be ruled by a king. They kept that oath, in name, for the rest of their history, and broke it in substance within five centuries.

The government they devised in place of the kings was called the res publica, a Latin phrase meaning the public thing, or the commonwealth, from which we take our word republic. It was not a democracy like that of Athens. Power was shared, in a balance that the Greek historian Polybius, who lived in Rome as a hostage, much admired, between three elements. There were the magistrates, chief among them two consuls, elected each year, who commanded the armies and presided over the state; each could forbid the acts of the other, and neither held power for more than a year. There was the Senate, a council of former magistrates, which had no formal power to make laws but whose advice, given by men of experience and family, was rarely disregarded. And there were the assemblies of the people, which elected the magistrates and passed the laws, but in which the votes were so arranged that the rich counted for more than the poor.

The early history of the Republic was dominated by what the Romans called the struggle of the orders, between the patricians, the old noble families, and the plebeians, everyone else. Step by step the plebeians won rights: their own officers, the tribunes, who could forbid any act of a magistrate against a plebeian; the publication of the laws, on twelve bronze tablets set up in the Forum, so that everyone might know them; and at last admission to all the offices of state. It was a slow and largely peaceful revolution, achieved partly by the plebeians' habit of simply withdrawing from the city, like a modern strike, until their demands were met.

The Republic was a machine for war, and it conquered almost without pause. By two hundred and seventy years before Christ it ruled all Italy. Then it fought three wars with Carthage, the great Phoenician city of North Africa, for mastery of the western Mediterranean. In the second of these, the Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps with his army and his elephants and destroyed Roman army after Roman army in Italy, killing perhaps fifty thousand Romans in a single afternoon at Cannae in two hundred and sixteen. The Romans did not ask for peace. They raised new armies, and wore him down, and at last beat him in Africa. In one hundred and forty-six they destroyed Carthage utterly, and in the same year destroyed Corinth in Greece. The Mediterranean had become, as they later called it, our sea.

Conquest brought wealth beyond imagining, and the wealth destroyed the Republic. The Roman army had been made up of small farmers, who served in the campaigning season and went home to their fields. The long wars overseas kept them away for years; their farms fell into debt and were bought up by rich men, who worked them with slaves captured in the same wars. The soldier-farmers drifted to Rome and became a hungry city mob. When two brothers, the Gracchi, tried as tribunes to give land back to the poor, in the years one hundred and thirty-three and one hundred and twenty-three before Christ, both were killed by mobs of senators and their followers. Blood had been shed in the politics of Rome, and it would not stop.

Generals began to recruit armies of landless men, who looked to their commander, not to the state, for pay and for land on their discharge. Such armies would follow their general anywhere, even against Rome. Marius and Sulla fought civil wars in the eighties before Christ, and Sulla made himself dictator and published lists of his enemies, who could be killed by anyone for a reward. The constitution survived, but as a shell.

Gaius Julius Caesar was born into an old but impoverished patrician family about one hundred years before Christ. He was a man of extraordinary talents: an orator second only to Cicero, a writer of the clearest Latin prose ever composed, a politician of genius, and the ablest general of his age. He was also immensely ambitious and wholly unscrupulous in his borrowing, owing at one point sums so vast that his creditors had a strong interest in his success. As governor of Gaul, from fifty-eight to fifty years before Christ, he conquered the whole of what is now France and Belgium, at the cost, by the ancient writers' own reckoning, of a million Gallic lives, and twice crossed into Britain, with indifferent success. His account of these wars, the Commentaries on the Gallic War, has been read by every schoolboy in Europe, generally under compulsion.

When the Senate ordered him to give up his army, in forty-nine, he crossed the little river Rubicon, the boundary of his province, into Italy, with the words, as reported, the die is cast, and began a civil war against Pompey and the Senate. He won it. He made himself dictator, at last dictator for life, and began reforms, among them the reform of the calendar, which, with a small correction by Pope Gregory in fifteen eighty-two, we still use. On the Ides of March, the fifteenth day, in forty-four, he was stabbed to death in a meeting of the Senate by some sixty senators, led by Brutus and Cassius, who believed they were restoring the Republic.

They were not. Thirteen more years of civil war followed, at the end of which Caesar's adopted heir Octavian, having defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra, made himself master of the Roman world. He took the name Augustus, meaning revered, and was careful never to call himself king. He called himself merely first citizen, and restored, he said, the Republic. Mr Gibbon observed of him that he was sensible that mankind is governed by names. The Republic, in name, lasted for centuries more. In substance, it had died with Caesar.
